questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: In October 2026 RBI announced that Paytm Payments Bank Limited had been excluded from which schedule?

options.text: The Third Schedule to the Banking Regulation Act, 1949
The Second Schedule to the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934
The First Schedule to the SEBI Act, 1992
The Schedule to the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007

solution.explanation: Banks included in the Second Schedule to the RBI Act, 1934 are 'scheduled banks'. Paytm Payments Bank was excluded from it by a notification dated 31 July 2026, published in the Gazette on 7 September 2026; RBI announced this on 7 October 2026.
steps: Scheduled status ↔ Second Schedule, RBI Act 1934 → Paytm PB excluded

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's Payments Banks – Digital Banking Channels Authorisation Directions, 2025, how does a payments bank start a 'view only' internet or mobile banking facility, compared with a 'transactional' facility?

options.text: Both need RBI's prior approval
Neither needs any approval or intimation
View-only needs RBI's prior approval; transactional needs only Board approval
View-only: with Board approval, intimating RBI within 30 days with a GAICA report; transactional: only with RBI's prior approval

solution.explanation: Banks with CBS and IPv6-enabled public-facing IT may offer view-only facilities, intimating RBI's Department of Regulation through PRAVAAH within thirty days of the Board-approved decision, along with a Gap Assessment and Internal Controls Adequacy (GAICA) report. A transactional facility needs RBI's prior approval.
solution.why_others_wrong: The two facilities are treated differently; the last option reverses them.
solution.final_answer: Option D: View-only: with Board approval, intimating RBI within 30 days with a GAICA report; transactional: only with RBI's prior approval

fact_checks.claim: The banks commencing view only digital banking channel(s) ... shall intimate the Department of Regulation, Reserve Bank of India (through the PRAVAAH portal) along with a copy of the 'Gap Assessment and Internal Controls Adequacy' (GAICA) report ... within thirty days from the decision to launch the facility with the approval of bank board
Banks shall require prior approval of the Reserve Bank for launching transactional banking facility

questions.question_text: According to RBI's Small Finance Banks – Licensing Guidelines, 2025, small finance banks are set up to further financial inclusion mainly through:

options.text: Large-ticket corporate lending and investment banking
Payments and remittances only, without any lending

Savings vehicles for unserved and underserved people, and credit to small businesses, small and marginal farmers, micro and small industries and the unorganised sector, through high technology–low cost operations
Financing of infrastructure projects through long-term bonds

steps: Savings for underserved + small-ticket credit, low-cost technology

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A newly licensed small finance bank commences business in October. Under the SFB Licensing Guidelines, 2025, how is its first priority sector target set?

options.text: On its first audited balance sheet as on 31 March, applying to the following year; it cannot sell PSL Certificates in the intervening period
On its opening balance sheet, applying from day one
At 40% of ANBC for the first three years
It has no PSL target for the first five years

solution.concept: First PSL target of an SFB
solution.explanation: The first audited balance sheet as on 31 March after commencement forms the basis of the first PSL target, for the subsequent financial year. In the intervening period (commencement to that 31 March) the SFB is not allowed to sell PSLCs.
steps: Basis: first audited 31 March balance sheet
solution.why_others_wrong: There is no day-one target, no 40% transitional rate and no five-year holiday.
solution.final_answer: Option A: On its first audited balance sheet as on 31 March, applying to the following year; it cannot sell PSL Certificates in the intervening period

fact_checks.claim: The first audited balance sheet as on March 31st, post commencement of operations of the small finance bank, would form the basis for the first PSL target for the bank (for the subsequent financial year). During the 'intervening period' ... the small finance banks are not allowed to sell Priority Sector Lending Certificates

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: What capital adequacy requirement applies to small finance banks under the SFB Licensing Guidelines, 2025?

options.text: CRAR of 9%, as for other commercial banks
CRAR of 12%, with no separate Tier I floor
CRAR of 15%, with Tier II capped at 50% of Tier I
CRAR of at least 15% on a continuous basis, Tier I at least 7.5% of RWAs, and Tier II capped at 100% of Tier I

solution.explanation: SFBs must maintain minimum CRAR of 15% of RWAs continuously; Tier I capital must be at least 7.5% of RWAs; Tier II is limited to 100% of Tier I.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9% and 12% are not the SFB requirement; the Tier II cap is 100% of Tier I, not 50%.
solution.final_answer: Option D: CRAR of at least 15% on a continuous basis, Tier I at least 7.5% of RWAs, and Tier II capped at 100% of Tier I

fact_checks.claim: The small finance bank shall be required to maintain a minimum capital adequacy ratio of 15 per cent of its risk weighted assets (RWA) on a continuous basis ... Tier I capital should be at least 7.5 per cent of RWAs. Tier II capital should be limited to a maximum of 100 per cent of total Tier I capital

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A small finance bank has risk-weighted assets of ₹8,000 crore, Tier I capital of ₹560 crore and Tier II capital of ₹700 crore. Applying the SFB capital norms, which statement is correct?

options.text: CRAR is 15.75%, so the bank complies
Eligible Tier II is capped at ₹560 crore, so CRAR is 14% and Tier I is 7%; both requirements are breached
CRAR is 15.75% but Tier I at 7% is short
CRAR is 14% but Tier I at 7% meets the 7% floor

solution.explanation: Tier II counts only up to 100% of Tier I: min(700, 560) = 560. CRAR = (560 + 560) ÷ 8,000 = 14% < 15%. Tier I ratio = 560 ÷ 8,000 = 7% < 7.5%. Both are breached.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15.75% ignores the Tier II cap; the Tier I floor is 7.5%, not 7%.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Eligible Tier II is capped at ₹560 crore, so CRAR is 14% and Tier I is 7%; both requirements are breached

fact_checks.claim: minimum capital adequacy ratio of 15 per cent ... Tier I capital should be at least 7.5 per cent of RWAs. Tier II capital should be limited to a maximum of 100 per cent of total Tier I capital

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
An NBFC that has secured borrowings backed by a floating charge on its assets converts into a small finance bank. Consider:
I. SFBs are precluded from creating floating charges on their assets.
II. The existing floating-charge borrowings may be grandfathered till maturity.
III. The assets under such a charge carry no extra risk weight.
Which of the above is/are correct under the SFB Licensing Guidelines, 2025?

options.text: I and II only
II and III only
I and III only
I, II and III

solution.explanation: SFBs cannot create floating charges. For a converting NBFC/MFI, such borrowings on the balance sheet on conversion day are grandfathered till maturity, but an additional 25% risk weight is imposed on the assets on which the charge/lien was created. So III is wrong.
solution.why_others_wrong: Any option with III is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: I and II only

fact_checks.claim: SFBs are precluded from creating floating charge on their assets. For such NBFCs / MFIs ... if they have created floating charges on their assets for secured borrowings ... RBI will permit grandfathering of such borrowings till their maturity. An additional risk weight of 25 per cent will be imposed on the assets on which charge / lien has been created by the converting entity

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: On 9 October 2026, after reviewing liquidity conditions, RBI announced an OMO sale of government securities worth ₹25,000 crore. What is the effect of an OMO sale on banking system liquidity?

options.text: It injects liquidity, as RBI pays the buyers
It absorbs liquidity, as buyers pay RBI for the securities
It has no effect, as it only changes ownership among banks
It raises the CRR automatically

solution.explanation: In an OMO sale RBI sells G-secs; buyers pay from their accounts, so reserves move to RBI and liquidity is absorbed. The 13 October 2026 auction offered six securities (2030–2034 maturities) through a multi-security, multiple-price auction.
steps: OMO sale → funds flow to RBI → liquidity absorbed
solution.why_others_wrong: OMO purchases inject liquidity; a sale is not neutral; CRR is set separately.
solution.final_answer: Option B: It absorbs liquidity, as buyers pay RBI for the securities

fact_checks.claim: On a review of current and evolving liquidity conditions, the Reserve Bank has decided to conduct an OMO sale auction of Government of India securities for an aggregate amount of ₹25,000 crore on October 13, 2026, through multi-security auction using the multiple price method

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: On 19 October 2026 the Government ran a switch auction of ₹20,000 crore, exchanging securities maturing in 2027–2029 for securities maturing between 2033 and 2060. What is the main purpose of such a switch?

options.text: To raise fresh borrowing of ₹20,000 crore
To inject liquidity into the banking system
To ease near-term redemption pressure by lengthening the maturity profile of debt
To convert dated securities into Treasury Bills

solution.explanation: A switch exchanges existing (source) securities for other (destination) securities without fresh borrowing. Replacing 2027–2029 papers with 2033–2060 papers spreads redemptions and lengthens the debt's maturity, reducing rollover risk.
steps: No fresh money; maturity profile lengthened
solution.why_others_wrong: A switch raises no fresh money, is not a liquidity operation, and does not create T-bills.
solution.final_answer: Option C: To ease near-term redemption pressure by lengthening the maturity profile of debt

fact_checks.claim: Government of India announces the conversion/switch of its securities through auction for an aggregate amount of ₹20,000 crore (face value) ... Source Securities 8.26% GS 2027 ... 6.79% GS 2029; Destination Securities 7.19% GS 2060 ... 7.57% GS 2033

Which statement is correct?

6.10% GS 2031 made up the largest share, about 37.7%
Each security was sold in equal amounts of about ₹4,167 crore
The full ₹25,000 crore was sold, and 7.18% GS 2033 alone made up about 37.7% of it

solution.why_others_wrong: The total is 25,000, not 22,000; 6.10% GS 2031 (8,430) was second; amounts were unequal.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: RBI announced that Floating Rate Bond 2034 will pay 7.26% a year for the half year 30 October 2026 to 29 April 2027. The coupon equals a base rate plus a fixed spread of 0.98%. What base rate does this imply, and how is it set?

options.text: 6.28%: the average of the weighted average yields of the last three 182-day T-bill auctions before the rate-fixing day
6.28%: the repo rate on the rate-fixing day
8.24%: the 10-year G-sec yield plus spread
7.26%: the average 364-day T-bill cut-off yield

solution.explanation: Base rate = coupon − spread = 7.26 − 0.98 = 6.28%. For FRB 2034 the base is the average of the WAY of the last three 182-day T-bill auctions from the rate-fixing day, and the coupon resets every half-year.
steps: Base = avg WAY of last three 182-day T-bill auctions
solution.why_others_wrong: The repo rate, 10-year yield and 364-day bill are not the reference; 8.24% adds instead of subtracts.
solution.final_answer: Option A: 6.28%: the average of the weighted average yields of the last three 182-day T-bill auctions before the rate-fixing day

fact_checks.claim: The rate of interest on Government of India Floating Rate Bond 2034 (FRB 2034) applicable for the half year October 30, 2026 to April 29, 2027 shall be 7.26 per cent per annum ... base rate equivalent to the average of the Weighted Average Yield (WAY) of last three auctions ... of 182 Day T-Bills, plus a fixed spread (0.98 per cent)

questions.question_text: Under RBI's Certificate of Deposit Directions, 2021, on what basis are CDs issued?

options.text: T+1, where T is the date on which the offer period for the CD issue closes
T+4, where T is the deal date
T+0 only, on the date of the board resolution
T+7, where T is the date of application to RBI

solution.explanation: CDs are issued on a T+1 basis, T being the date of closure of the offer period. (Primary CP and NCD issues, by contrast, may settle up to T+4 working days.) CDs are in demat form only.
steps: CD issue: T+1 from offer closure
solution.why_others_wrong: T+4 is the CP/NCD primary settlement limit; the other bases are not in the Directions.
solution.final_answer: Option A: T+1, where T is the date on which the offer period for the CD issue closes

fact_checks.claim: CDs shall be issued on a T+1 basis where T represents the date of closure of the offer period for issuance of the CDs

questions.question_text: How may commercial paper (CP) be priced at issue under RBI's Directions of 2024?

options.text: At a discount or with a fixed coupon
Only at a discount to face value
Only with a floating coupon linked to the repo rate
At par, with interest paid on maturity

solution.explanation: CPs shall be issued at a discount to the face value. Short-term NCDs, in contrast, may be issued at a discount or with a fixed or floating coupon.

solution.why_others_wrong: Coupon-bearing issue (fixed or floating) is allowed for NCDs, not CPs; CP is not issued at par with interest.

questions.question_text: In any primary issuance of commercial paper or short-term NCDs, what is the limit on subscription by individuals under RBI's 2024 Directions?

options.text: Individuals cannot subscribe at all
Each individual may take up to ₹5 lakh only
All individuals together, including HUFs, may not take more than 25% of the amount issued
Individuals together may take up to 50% of the amount issued

solution.explanation: All residents (and non-residents to the extent FEMA permits) may invest in CPs and NCDs, but total subscription by all individuals, including Hindu Undivided Families, in a primary issuance cannot exceed 25% of the total amount issued. ₹5 lakh is the minimum denomination, not a cap.
solution.why_others_wrong: Individuals are not barred; ₹5 lakh is the minimum denomination; 50% is not the limit.
solution.final_answer: Option C: All individuals together, including HUFs, may not take more than 25% of the amount issued

fact_checks.claim: Total subscription by all individuals, including Hindu Undivided Families, in any primary issuance of CPs or NCDs shall not exceed 25 per cent of the total amount issued

questions.question_text: A company defaults on the redemption of its commercial paper. What must it do under RBI's 2024 Directions?

options.text: Inform RBI within 30 days and nothing more
Roll the CP over automatically for one month
Inform only the credit rating agency at its next review
Inform the IPA before 5:00 pm on the day of default and publicly disseminate the default, e.g. on its website

solution.explanation: An issuer that defaults on a coupon or redemption of a CP/NCD must inform the IPA before 5:00 pm on the date of default (and the debenture trustee for NCDs) and publicly disseminate the default. The IPA reports it on CCIL's F-TRAC platform by 5:30 pm, and the issuer cannot issue CPs/NCDs until it repays or six months pass.
steps: IPA reports on F-TRAC by 5:30 pm
solution.why_others_wrong: Automatic rollover is not allowed, and RBI-only or rating-agency-only intimation is not the rule.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Inform the IPA before 5:00 pm on the day of default and publicly disseminate the default, e.g. on its website

fact_checks.claim: The issuer who has defaulted on the repayment of a coupon/redemption, partially or in full, of a CP and/or NCD shall inform the details of any default in payments related to a CP/NCD to the IPA before 5:00 pm on the date of the default ... questions.question_text: Under RBI's 2024 Directions, within what time must a primary issuance of commercial paper be settled, i.e. funds paid to the issuer and CPs issued to investors?

options.text: On the same day (T+0) only
Within T+4 working days of the deal date
Within T+1 working day of the deal date
Within 15 days of the board resolution

solution.explanation: Primary issuances of CPs and NCDs, including both payment of funds and issue of the instruments, must be settled within T+4 working days, where T is the date on which the trade details including price are agreed. Secondary OTC trades settle T+0 or T+1, and CDs are issued on a T+1 basis.
solution.why_others_wrong: T+0/T+1 is the secondary-market settlement cycle; T+1 applies to CD issuance; the board resolution is not the reference date.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Within T+4 working days of the deal date

fact_checks.claim: The primary issuances of CPs and NCDs ... shall be settled within a period not exceeding T+4 working days, where T represents the deal date
The settlement cycle for OTC trades in CPs and NCDs shall be either T+0 or T+1

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT permitted while issuing commercial paper under RBI's 2024 Directions?

options.text: Issuing the CP with a call or put option
Credit enhancement by a bank through a stand-by facility
Issuing the CP in dematerialised form
Appointing a scheduled commercial bank as Issuing and Paying Agent

solution.explanation: Issuance of a CP/NCD with options (call/put) is not permitted, and it cannot be underwritten or co-accepted. Banks and AIFIs may provide credit enhancement such as stand-by assistance; CPs must be in demat form; and an IPA, which must be a scheduled commercial bank, is required for each issue.
solution.why_others_wrong: Credit enhancement is allowed; demat form and an SCB as IPA are mandatory.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Issuing the CP with a call or put option

questions.question_text: A company with an 'A2+' rating plans a ₹600 crore CP issue of 120 days. 2,400 individuals want to subscribe ₹10 lakh each, and an NBFC (a related party of the company) wants ₹100 crore. Applying RBI's 2024 Directions, which statement is correct?

options.text: Individuals can be allotted the full ₹240 crore, and the NBFC can take ₹100 crore
Individuals can be allotted at most ₹150 crore, and the NBFC can take ₹100 crore
The issue cannot be made, as an 'A2+' rating is below the minimum
Individuals can be allotted at most ₹150 crore in all, and the related NBFC cannot invest at all

solution.explanation: Individuals (including HUFs) may take at most 25% of a primary issue: 25% × 600 = ₹150 crore, so the ₹240 crore of demand (2,400 × ₹10 lakh) cannot be met in full. No person, resident or non-resident, may invest in CPs/NCDs issued by related parties. 'A2+' is above the minimum rating of A3, so the issue is allowed.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹240 crore exceeds the 25% cap; the related NBFC is barred; A2+ is better than the A3 minimum.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Individuals can be allotted at most ₹150 crore in all, and the related NBFC cannot invest at all

questions.question_text:
Consider the following statements about RBI's 2024 Directions on CPs and short-term NCDs:
I. The issuer must make funds for redemption available to the IPA by 3:00 pm on the redemption date.
II. The debenture trustee reports outstanding NCDs and defaults to RBI quarterly, within 15 days of the quarter's end.
III. Depositories report CP and NCD holdings to RBI only once a quarter.
Which of the above is/are correct?

options.text: II and III only
I and III only
I and II only
I, II and III

solution.concept: Repayment and reporting in CP/NCD markets
solution.explanation: I is correct: redemption funds must reach the IPA by 3:00 pm on the redemption date, and repayment is routed through the IPA. II is correct: the debenture trustee reports quarterly, within 15 days of the end of the quarter. III is wrong: depositories report fortnightly (on the 15th and the last day of the month).
solution.why_others_wrong: Any option containing III is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: I and II only

fact_checks.claim: The issuer shall make the funds for redemption available to the IPA by 3:00 P.M. on the redemption date

The Debenture Trustee shall report the details of the outstanding amount of NCDs and the particulars of default in repayment of NCD, at quarterly intervals (within 15 days from the end of the quarter)
The depositories shall report to the Reserve Bank, the details of the CPs and NCDs held with them ... at fortnightly intervals (on the 15th day and on the last day of the month)

questions.question_text: A company defaults on a CP redemption on 10 February 2027 and repays the defaulted amount in full on 20 May 2027. Under RBI's 2024 Directions, from when can it issue CPs or NCDs again?

options.text: From 10 August 2027, six months after the default, irrespective of repayment
From 20 May 2027, the date of full repayment, as that is earlier than six months after the default
Only after one year from the date of default
Only after a fresh rating of A1+ is obtained

solution.explanation: After a default, the issuer cannot issue CPs or NCDs till full repayment of the defaulted obligation or six months after the date of default, whichever is earlier. Full repayment (20 May 2027) comes before 10 August 2027, so the bar lifts on 20 May 2027. The default must also be reported to the IPA before 5 pm on the day of default and publicly disseminated.
solution.why_others_wrong: The six-month date applies only if repayment is later; there is no one-year bar or A1+ requirement.
solution.final_answer: Option B: From 20 May 2027, the date of full repayment, as that is earlier than six months after the default

fact_checks.claim: In the event of default of a CP / NCD, the issuer shall not be allowed to issue CPs or NCDs till full repayment of the defaulted obligation or six months after the date of default, whichever is earlier

Punjab, Haryana and the UT of Chandigarh, under SEBI's Northern Regional Office, New Delhi

options.text: The fortnightly average (about ₹10,006 crore) is adequate, but the ₹9,880 crore day breaches the daily floor of ₹9,900 crore
The bank complies fully, since the daily floor is ₹9,000 crore
The bank fails because its balance fell below ₹10,000 crore on two days
The bank fails because the fortnightly average is below ₹10,000 crore

solution.explanation: The average must be at least the required CRR, and every day's balance at least 99% of it. Average = (10,150 + 9,950 + 9,880 + 10,100 + 10 × 10,000) ÷ 14 ≈ ₹10,006 crore, which is adequate. Daily floor = 0.99 × 10,000 = ₹9,900 crore; the ₹9,880 crore day falls short, while ₹9,950 crore is within the floor.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹9,000 crore was the floor under the old 90% rule; balances between 99% and 100% on a day are allowed; the average is above the requirement.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The fortnightly average (about ₹10,006 crore) is adequate, but the ₹9,880 crore day breaches the daily floor of ₹9,900 crore
